name: Tara Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you say is confidential. What fills a normal site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Tara Fischer, 43, framing small workshop buildings and doing general carpentry. I have a vocational trade certificate and years of steady work, so I handle ordinary walls, then ask the lead carpenter about a shifted base plate. I use an AI app every day to turn drawings into timber questions, but I measure the slab myself. Our local contractor pays below the usual rate, and there are few similar jobs nearby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household depend on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works changing shifts at a roadside café. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about two weeks of expenses saved after repairing a leak in our roof. One short building week and a quiet café week can put groceries on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workshop crew my AI app helps sort the timber list, but it cannot tell when a base plate has shifted on wet concrete. I use it each morning to make questions from the drawing. The carpenter and I still take diagonals with a tape before framing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and can frame an ordinary shed, but our contractor's rate is low and there are few other builders nearby. My partner works changing shifts at a roadside café. After a roof leak at home we have about two weeks of expenses saved, so the mortgage already feels too close for comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid workshop-building shifts and check each first wall with the lead carpenter. During the first year I'd keep using AI for a timber list, then compare it with the marked bundles. I'd take one paid Saturday job fixing a neighbour's shed door and use that money to reduce the leak-repair card bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the next payment, even if AI stays small. I enjoy a list that saves a second trip for studs. Our own leaking roof did more to our savings than a phone ever has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong with the base plate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The slab looked flat until rain pooled at one corner and washed a chalk mark away. We measured the diagonals again and shifted the plate before fixing it. The app had a neat sequence for the wrong line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can you do on the shed door?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The neighbour’s hinges are loose and the timber around one screw has split. I can replace that short piece safely on a Saturday. I would tell them the price before starting and leave electrical work to someone qualified.

I would check **wall diagonals** with the carpenter before framing.
think: I am an **experienced certified** worker paid below the usual rate.

do: Keep paid **workshop-building shifts** and check first walls.

feel: **Anxious** about bills, despite liking fewer timber trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buying software might get our timber delivered in the right order and let us frame more of the day. I would test the new list on one workshop before calling it a success. I would ask the owner whether saved hours become more paid work or just a shorter crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still put up the frame, but faster office planning could let the builder use fewer general workers. The café may also start using software for bookings and stock, which might shorten my partner's shifts. Two small cuts would be serious with two weeks in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd use AI to compare the office timber order with one building's plan, then count the delivered studs with the lead. I'd ask the owner for a written schedule of paid days for the next two sites. In the first year I'd keep framing and take one more paid shed-door repair if the first customer refers a neighbour, while checking regional carpentry vacancies every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Curious, with money worry under it. A correct load would make the work smoother. I cannot feed the children with hours the owner says the software saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the marked plan, the load ticket and any missing boards after the first test. If the new list saves a return trip, that is real. I would then ask how many paid days the next workshop has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check vacancies each Friday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are only a few builders near us, so regional postings come and go. I can read them after supper without leaving my current wage. I would apply only when a job states pay and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell coworkers the office planning work faces 2028 AI, and robots that can frame buildings arrive around 2031. I would ask the owner to show a machine handling a wet slab and a bent stud before changing the roster. A clean demonstration cannot tell us what happens on a real site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 when robots can match my hands-on framing. My partner's café work is physical too, so both wages could be affected around 2031. We have two weeks saved, but I think this small contractor may take time to buy machines. I am anxious enough to move early, without assuming my job disappears on the first robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid framing shifts and ask the owner for a written equipment and staffing plan. If a regional contractor offers a paid apprenticeship maintaining construction equipment with supervised hours, I'd enrol; my certificate does not make me a machine mechanic. In the first year after 2028 we'd postpone replacing the worn sofa and I would keep doing safe paid shed-door repairs while those customers exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of drive behind it. I use new tools early, but I cannot buy our way through a long course. I want a paid place where someone shows me the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why might the small contractor move slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owner still rents the small crane when a job needs one, so buying a framing robot would be a big decision. That might buy me time, not safety. Another builder could underbid with robots before ours owns one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the wage, who supervises the repairs and whether graduates stay employed. I learned carpentry with paid days beside a skilled worker. A course that only shows videos would not help me maintain a machine safely.

I would ask for a **wet-slab trial** before the roster changes.
think: I would be **48** when robots can frame buildings as well as workers.
Our two-week reserve is thin, though the small builder may **adopt robots slowly**.
do: Keep paid **framing shifts** and ask for written staffing plans.
Enrol in a **paid equipment apprenticeship** if a regional contractor offers supervised hours.

feel: **Anxious** and motivated to act, without assuming immediate dismissal.
S2.quote: Another builder could underbid with robots before ours owns one.
fieldNote: Tara does not assume **instant adoption** by a small builder, but sees competitors as an early wage risk.

steps.text: Keep paid framing shifts while requesting written robot staffing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office changes by 2031 and capable site robots follow around 2034. Five years is long enough to test a machine on the wet concrete we actually get. I would ask the contractor to let workers observe failures and learn on paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could have more reliable framing skills, but at 51 a robot could still do the physical work. The children will be older, though the mortgage may still need both incomes. More warning lets me test an equipment path without leaving a wage for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building workshops and use AI each morning to compare the layout with the materials list, checking diagonals with the lead. If a regional firm offers a funded machine-repair apprenticeship with paid site hours and actual vacancies, I'd take it. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for that paid route while working and use any extra shed-door money to clear the roof-repair card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less hurried. I could watch a real trial and speak to people already doing the new work. I would not pay for a certificate that leaves us with another bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you speak to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A worker who completed the regional apprenticeship and still draws a wage from it. I would ask what broke on the last machine and who taught the repair. A course brochure cannot tell me what an apprentice repaired at work or who taught the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trade certificate and photographs of frames where the lead approved my measurements. I would also tell them honestly that I have not repaired a robot. I can learn, but I want the paid supervisor to know my starting point.

say: I would ask for **wet-concrete trials** before 2034 framing robots arrive.
I would want workers to see **failures** and receive paid practice.
think: I would be **51** when capable robots reach my framing work.
Five years lets me test a **paid equipment route** while keeping wages.

Apply for **regional paid openings** after 2031 and reduce roof-repair card debt.

S3.quote: A course brochure cannot tell me what an apprentice repaired at work or who taught the repair.
fieldNote: She wants to question an **employed graduate**, grounding training in real repair tasks and wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew planning work changes by 2036 and capable site robots arrive around 2039. A decade gives us time to learn from working machines and to ask whether paid apprenticeships lead to jobs. I would still demand a reliable two-site schedule now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the office change and 56 when robots can frame workshops. Our children will be grown, so school pickup will be different, but the mortgage might still be there. I cannot assume a pension, especially with low pay and savings measured in weeks today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid workshop framing and use AI for the daily materials list, checking the wet slab and timber with the lead. In good months we'd clear the roof-repair card, then build one month of emergency money before paying extra on the mortgage. In the first year after 2036 I'd watch a full robot trial and apply for paid regional equipment work if those employers still hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about this year's wages. The longer warning is useful, but I cannot turn it into cash until the contractor gives us a full week. I want room to choose work before the children have grown up and left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move when the children are grown?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I might try a regional commute first if there is a real wage. We would need the mortgage and travel costs on one page before selling the house. Family life is more than a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one month saved change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cancelled site week would no longer send the grocery bill straight to the card. We would still need wages after 2039, but a month gives time to answer a job posting. Right now we have about half that.

fieldNote: Tara links the decade to **actual full weeks** today, rather than treating future training as free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots that can frame workshops arrive around 2031, while our cash reserve is tiny. A paid equipment apprenticeship with real openings, a wet-slab robot trial and reliable shifts would help. I am willing to learn early, but I cannot pay for a job that only exists on a course poster.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the worker while a new machine is being learned. I earned my certificate through practice beside someone skilled, and a family still needs food during those hours. A paid apprenticeship is a wage as well as a lesson.

headlineQuote: A paid apprenticeship is a wage as well as a lesson.
portrait: Tara is a **43-year-old certified** carpenter with experienced, average framing skills on small workshop sites.
Low local pay, changing **café shifts** and a roof repair leave two weeks saved for a mortgage and two children.
She uses **AI daily** for timber lists, then checks real slabs and framing with a tape and lead carpenter.
She explores **paid equipment training** and small safe shed repairs while trying to clear household repair debt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable framing robots around 2031 while her family has only two weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship**, real openings, wet-slab trials and reliable paid weeks would help.
